Subject: Post-demo: SLO confirmation & warm-pool questions

Thanks again for the time today — good chat. Quick written recap + ask so we have alignment before Marissa and Karthik put together the technical plan. Attaching a short MAPl PDF with the items we discussed. [attachment: 20261107-acme-ma-planned-warmpool.pdf]

Recap of the SLOs you described during the demo:
- Target P95 latency: <= 200ms for streaming responses (client sees first chunk within 80ms, subsequent chunks no more than 60ms apart)
- Peak request throughput (sustained): ~120 req/s
- Peak concurrency (interactive sessions): typical 60, expected campaign burst factor up to 30x for short periods
- Long-tail bursts: up to ~1.8k concurrent requests during promos we run ~2-3x per month

Open questions where we need confirmation from you (quick answers will help us size warm pool vs reserved capacity):
1) For the streaming requirement, is the P95 latency target strictly end-to-end (client->first-token) or are you willing to separate first-byte from steady-state chunk cadence?
2) For burst windows, what is the expected duration (seconds/minutes) and cadence (how often per month)?
3) Is some queueing acceptable for the very highest burst spikes (i.e., queue up to 500ms), or must we keep tail latency constant with immediate failures instead?
4) Do you have any hard constraints on model degradation (e.g., would you accept fallback to a slightly smaller model with identical prompt semantics for bursts)?

Next steps we propose:
- Marissa to draft warm-pool sizing + scale-up timeline options (cold start vs pre-warm)
- Karthik to recommend routing/fallback policy and cost tradeoffs (reserved vs burstable hosted)
- Schedule a 30-min technical review next week to finalize the MAPl and a pilot timeline

If you can answer Q1-4 inline that would be ideal. Thanks!

—Camila
Camila Reyes
Senior Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Post-demo: SLO confirmation & warm-pool questions

Camila — thanks for the clear recap. Confirming the numbers with the product team, and answering inline: 

Q1: We care most about the user-perceived first-byte/first-token for chat — so P95 for first-token <=200ms is our primary SLO. Separate cadence for steady-state is acceptable; we expect ~40–80ms between chunks after the first token.
Q2: Burst windows are short: typically 60–180 seconds, but can repeat across an hour for big campaigns. Average once/month, heavy quarter activity 2–3x/month.
Q3: We prefer not to queue more than ~250–300ms; anything longer starts to hurt conversions. If queueing is used it should be visible/measureable.
Q4: We are open to fallback to a slightly smaller model as long as hallucination risk doesn't materially increase; we need to see quality delta on our eval set.

Also: two operational asks — can you provide an estimate for (a) warm-pool fill time (how long to go from 0->desired hot instances) and (b) cost delta between reserved hot pool vs autoscaling with pre-warm + burstable shared capacity?

Happy to do the technical review next Thu 11/12. 

-Jamie
Head of Product, Acme AI
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>

Subject: RE: Post-demo: SLO confirmation & warm-pool questions (technical notes)

Looping in the technical plan based on Camila's recap + Jamie's clarifications. High-level notes and numbers we will validate in a short runbook: 

1) Interpretation of SLOs- We will target P95 first-token <=200ms (client-observed) and steady-state chunk cadence 40–80ms. We'll record both metrics separately in the console.

2) Warm pool sizing logic (initial proposal)- Typical concurrency: 60 -> baseline hot pool of ~8 worker replicas (each replica handles ~8 concurrent streams at target throughput with tokenization and KV cache warmed)
- Burst factor: 30x short bursts (1.8k concurrent) -> add a configurable warm buffer size of 120 hot replicas to cover 60% of burst with headroom; remaining can be handled via rapid scale-up + short queueing/fallbacks.
- Expected buffer effectiveness: if warm pool covers ~60–70% of short bursts, observed scale-up demand will be much lower.

3) Scale-up timing- Cold boot (no warm pool): 90–120s to get full GPU worker up and serving (OS + runtime + model load).
- Pre-warmed container with model on disk but not resident in GPU: ~30–45s to jIT to GPU and load weights into GPU memory (depending on model quantization).
- Warm-pool (GPU resident): immediate (<500ms) for new incoming requests.

4) Queueing and fallbacks- We recommend allowing short queueing up to 250ms for the rarest spikes (fits your 250–300ms preference).
- For sustained overflow, route to a fallback model (same prompt semantics) with documented reduced context length to keep latency within SLO. We'll produce eval delta for your prompt set.

5) Cost tradeoffs (short summary)- Reserved hot pool: predictable cost, simplest to guarantee tight tail SLOs; recommended if you want <200ms P95 with no queueing during promos.
- Autoscale + pre-warm: lower committed cost, better average unit economics, requires thoughtful warm pool size + slightly higher tail risk.

6) Data/telemetry we'll deliver for pilot- P95 first-token, P50/P99 for chunk cadence, queueing time distribution, warm-pool hit rate, scale-up time per event.

I'll produce a concrete warm-pool sizing spreadsheet + cost compare (reserved vs pre-warm+burst) and attach as CSV. [attachment: slo-latency-examples.csv]

If this looks reasonable we can use Thu 11/12 10:00 PT for the technical review. Camila — can you lock that in with Jamie?

—Marissa
